results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 65 outline summaries of prose units match the controlling ideas of the spec paragraphs they align to, in spec order (p01-p65, with p40 and p41 inside the control points as declared); the five 'Introduction callout' entries are callouts, not spec paragraphs.

Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Forty-Eight Minutes on a Sunday Evening ¶4 (p08) was marked two_ideas, but the spec's controlling idea joins the review's cost and Ingrid's question in one paragraph; the cost sets up the question.

Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶8 (p24) was marked two_ideas, but the spec paragraph is 'two brown-out lessons apply to caching'; warming and key normalization are its two declared lessons.
Capacity Planning for Known Peaks ¶2 (p26) was marked two_ideas, but the spec paragraph defines the model 'counting queries as results-page requests'; fixing the unit is part of the definition.
From Platform to Leadership ¶2 (p64) was marked two_ideas, but the spec paragraph states the part's shared contract shape and that it answers the part's opening test for the city bike; one idea.

Every prose unit ties to a supporting claim: introduction and scene to S1/S2, traffic to S1, journeys to S2, control points to S3/S5 (p40-p41 to S5), capacity to S3, degradation and regions to S4, incidents to S2/S4, cost to S6, worked example and judging sections to S2-S6, conclusion to the part closing.

Each spec evidence item appears with a sentence saying what it shows: Rightmove (documented marketing peak), Vinted autumn ('None of this is surprising'), Imperva (caveated as whole-web vendor figures), the SRE definitions and retry rules, the journey table (p16 'Three design choices in that table'), the cache, ladder, region-options, baseline, worked-example, trade-off and vertical tables (each followed or introduced by an interpreting sentence), AWS us-east-1 (two lessons), Adevinta incidents ('its failure modes reach every tenant at once') and FinOps levers (p46), the OLX pointer marked as not evidence, and the capacity figures ('The cheapest capacity is the request that never reaches the cluster').

Declared contrast carrying over 'trade-offs that hold for every vertical' and introducing 'where the verticals differ'. The opening is additive ('too') and picks up nothing from the trade-offs section, so the reader is not told what the verticals differ from; reader-flow-1 asked 'Differ from what?'.

All other boundaries (p02-p65 and every section's transition_in) express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information, e.g. 'The architecture should first have known the traffic shape', 'The traffic shape says when load arrives, not which journeys matter', 'Control points protect those objectives', 'What the controls do not absorb, the backend must hold', 'Load can exceed even a rehearsed plan', 'Losing a site is degradation's larger form', 'Incidents still happen', 'Shedding, caching and headroom change spending', 'The redesign worked; the table says when each choice would not', 'Preventing those failures takes group decisions', 'These test those decisions', 'This chapter closes [[part-7]].'

Both flow readers describe the declared order: the brown-out as the problem, then load, journey objectives, protections in prerequisite order (control points, capacity, degradation, regions, incidents), cost, the rerun as the test, then the judging sections as grouped back matter. No section is unclear to both readers.

results.quote: It sets out the load (traffic shape, automated traffic included), what reliability means (journey objectives), what protects it (control points with the bot controls at the edge, capacity, degradation, regions, incidents) and what it costs.
results.finding: Both readers had to re-read the roadmap: nested parentheses and the compressed 'control points with the bot controls at the edge', followed by a bare list of the back-matter sections with no reason for their order. The spec order is fine; the sentence form obscures it.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶2
results.quote: The first control point is the edge, where automated traffic is classified, and policy for it starts from why bots come.
results.finding: The bot subsection restarts the introduction of bots instead of picking up the groups the traffic section already named; reader-flow-1 re-read the sentence (two ideas joined by 'and', ambiguous 'it'), reader-flow-2 read the motive paragraph as 'a second introduction to bots'. The spec places this material here deliberately; the prose should link back to the traffic section's groups rather than start again.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶4
results.quote: Behind the edge, the brown-out happened because interactive queries, reindexing and cache warm-up shared the same nodes at the same time.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this opener: 'Behind the edge' reads as modifying 'the brown-out happened' rather than naming the next control point.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶6
results.quote: OLX is reported to have published a two-part post in 2021 on load shedding with NGINX using adaptive concurrency control; it could not be retrieved or verified for this book, so treat it as a pointer, not evidence.
results.finding: Both readers report that the sourcing caveat interrupts the retries-and-admission argument and reads like an editorial note left in the text. The spec only asks that it be marked as a pointer; its placement and wording mid-argument are the draft's.

results.quote: Figures here count queries, meaning results-page requests; each query fans out to about 2.6 engine requests at Tradeyard
results.finding: The unit switches between 'search requests', 'queries', 'searches' and 'engine requests' (cost per thousand searches vs the table's 'Cost per 1,000 queries'), and the 2.6 fan-out is never used; reader-flow-1 was unsure whether the 13,000 figures were queries or engine requests, reader-flow-2 waited for the 2.6 to be applied and re-checked whether searches and queries are the same unit.

Reader-flow-1 marks the position of Vertical Differences 'somewhat unclear' ('Nothing in the trade-offs leads to it'); reader-flow-2 calls it 'loosely attached', with 'The verticals differ too' as its only link. The grouping order is fine; the bridge does not say how the section follows the trade-offs.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Forty-Eight Minutes on a Sunday Evening ¶5
results.quote: The "Sunday-evening peak" is a Veldmark illustration; the documented public example of a marketing-driven peak is Rightmove's
results.finding: Reader-flow-1 item 1: the evidence paragraph sits between Ingrid's question and the section that starts answering it and 'deflates the pivot'. The placement is the spec's (p09 closes the scene).

results.finding: Reader-flow-1 item 2: the announced control-point list does not match the subsections that follow (caching is not announced; 'degrade at a gateway' is covered under Graceful Degradation), so the reader had to re-map it.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶3
results.quote: this chapter's concern is that the policy is enforced at the edge and that automated traffic has its own capacity class
results.finding: Reader-flow-1 item 5: the bot subsection's commercial, legal and AI-licensing material drifts away from the search path, the one place the reader lost the reliability thread.

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶1
results.quote: reported separately for human and automated traffic
results.finding: Reader-flow-2 item 14: the definition promises cost per search split into human and automated traffic, and the baseline table does not split it.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶1
results.quote: keep batch work out of peak windows with the peak calendar set out under capacity planning
results.finding: 'Peak and campaign calendar' is on the spec's does_not_know list and is defined only in Capacity Planning (p29), but it is used here, in the Figure 3 caption and in isolation rule 1 ('by a calendar the platform enforces') before it is introduced. Both flow readers reported the forward reference.

The other does_not_know terms are defined at or before first use: SLI, SLO, error budget and critical user journey (p14), journey SLO (p15), peak window (p18), degradation mode (p31), peak rehearsal (p30), cost per search and unit economics (p42). Names the readers stopped at (Femke, the Rotterdam city bike, Yardstick, Common Ground, Fast Mail for Fraudsters, the register of copies, the part's opening test) are on the audience's already_knows list.
The introduction opens with a direct statement of the chapter's stance and the traffic shape, not a placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, 'dawn of man' or book report.
The conclusion opens by calling back to Ingrid's question, does not say 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or body evidence, and ends on a hand-off rather than a rephrased thesis.

p63 states that one piece of knowledge (which journeys make liquidity and when) sets objectives, calendar, ladder order and unit costs, which no single section states; p65 gives the so-what: building the contracts across acquired brands is a problem of change Part VIII takes up.

p63 returns to Ingrid's question ('Ingrid asked why nothing knew that Sunday at 20:35 mattered'); p64 returns to the part's opening test and answers it for the Rotterdam city bike with the listing-gone objective as the check.

The cold reader predicted the brown-out framing, the order load, journey objectives, control points with bot controls at the edge, capacity, degradation, regions, incidents, cost, then the rerun and back matter, and the evidence (SRE, Vinted, Adevinta, Rightmove, FinOps, bot reports, fictional Veldmark). Its uncertainties (where the brown-out is told, whether control points are a section) do not change the predicted sections.

The cold reader names a search journey objective counting human requests with a separate peak-window report and a budget policy restricting changes, a peak and campaign calendar marketing joins that blocks batch work, the ladder bots-optional-freshness-search, a gateway retry budget with jitter, bot classification at the edge and cost per thousand searches split by human and automated traffic. Only 'per owner' is not stated explicitly.

p64 states that Part VII's eight chapters give each capability a published contract (from the listing event to the journey objective), an owner and a check, which no single chapter states; p65 says building them across acquired brands is a problem of change Part VIII takes up; p64 answers the part's opening test for the Rotterdam city bike. The list of contracts is compressed to its two ends rather than named in full.
